network-advanced-001.question: When an L2 switch receives a frame, which information does it record in its MAC address table?
choices: The frame's source MAC address and the port on which the frame arrived
The frame's destination MAC address and the port out of which the frame was sent
A pair made of an IP address in the frame and the MAC address that corresponds to it
network-advanced-001.explanation: An L2 switch looks at the source MAC address of each frame it receives and records in its MAC address table that "this device is behind this port" (learning). To forward a frame, it looks up the destination MAC address in the table; if there is an entry it sends the frame only out of that port, and if not it sends it out of every port except the one it arrived on (flooding). The destination MAC address says nothing about where that device is, so it cannot be used for learning. An entry is removed if no frame arrives from that device for a set time (for example 300 seconds), so the table can follow devices that move.
choiceNotes: Correct. The source address tells the switch which port the device is behind.
The destination MAC address does not tell the switch which port the destination is behind. Learning uses the source address.
The mapping between IP and MAC addresses is what hosts and routers look up with ARP and keep (the ARP table).

network-advanced-002.question: An L2 switch with an empty MAC address table has devices on ports 1 to 4, all in the same VLAN. PC-A on port 1 sends a frame to PC-B on port 2, and PC-B then sends a reply frame to PC-A. How are the two frames forwarded?
choices: The first frame is sent only to port 2, and the reply is sent to ports 1, 3 and 4
The first frame is sent to ports 2, 3 and 4, and the reply is sent only to port 1
Both frames are sent out of every port except the one they arrived on
network-advanced-002.explanation: When the first frame arrives, the switch does not yet know PC-B's MAC address, so it sends the frame out of ports 2, 3 and 4, every port except port 1 where it arrived (flooding). At the same time, it learns that the sender, PC-A, is behind port 1. The reply is addressed to PC-A, which is already in the table, so it is sent only to port 1. The switch also learns that PC-B is behind port 2, so later frames between the two PCs are not flooded. The devices on ports 3 and 4 receive the first frame but discard it because the destination MAC address is not theirs.
choiceNotes: PC-B has not been learned yet, so the first frame cannot be sent to port 2 alone. By the time of the reply, PC-A has been learned.
Correct. Frames to unknown destinations are flooded, and frames to learned destinations go only to their port.
The first frame taught the switch where PC-A is, so the reply is not flooded.

network-advanced-003.question: An L2 switch with four PCs is connected to one interface of a router. A repeater hub with three PCs is connected to the router's other interface. No VLANs are used. Counting a collision domain as the range in which frames can collide on half-duplex Ethernet, which is the correct pair of numbers of broadcast domains and collision domains?
network-advanced-003.explanation: A router does not forward broadcasts, so each router interface is a separate broadcast domain, giving two here. An L2 switch makes each port a separate collision domain, so on the switch side the four PC ports and the port to the router are five separate collision domains. A repeater hub simply repeats signals to all its ports, so the hub, its three PCs and the router interface form one collision domain. That gives 5 + 1 = 6 in total. Today switches are normally connected in full duplex, and collisions cannot occur at all on a full-duplex link.
choiceNotes: This counts the whole switch as one collision domain. A switch makes each port its own collision domain.
Correct. The router splits the network into two broadcast domains, and there are five collision domains on the switch side and one on the hub side.
This mixes up the numbers of broadcast and collision domains. Routers stop broadcasts; switches and hubs do not.

network-advanced-004.question: The VLAN ID in an IEEE 802.1Q tag is 12 bits long, and the values 0 and 4095 are reserved for special purposes. How many VLAN IDs can be used to identify VLANs?
network-advanced-004.explanation: 12 bits can represent 2^12 = 4096 values (0 to 4095). Excluding 0, which is used for tags that carry only a priority, and the reserved value 4095 leaves 4096 − 2 = 4094 IDs for identifying VLANs. An 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes long and is inserted after the source MAC address in an Ethernet frame. It consists of a 2-byte value marking it as a tag (0x8100), a 3-bit priority (PCP), a 1-bit DEI and the 12-bit VLAN ID.
choiceNotes: This excludes only 0. The value 4095 is reserved as well.
This is the total number of 12-bit values, without excluding the two reserved ones.

network-advanced-005.question: Switches SW1 and SW2 both have ports in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. The two switches are to be connected with a single cable so that devices in the same VLAN can communicate across the switches. Which configuration of the connecting ports is appropriate?
choices: On both switches, make the connecting port an access port in VLAN 10
Remove VLAN 20, merge it into VLAN 10, and make the connecting port an access port in VLAN 10
On both switches, make the connecting port a trunk port and send frames with IEEE 802.1Q tags that identify their VLAN
network-advanced-005.explanation: An access port belongs to a single VLAN and is used to connect end devices. To carry frames from several VLANs over one link, the port is made a trunk port and each frame is sent with an IEEE 802.1Q tag holding its VLAN ID. The receiving switch reads the tag to tell which VLAN the frame belongs to and forwards it only to ports in that VLAN. One native VLAN can be chosen whose frames are sent untagged, and it must match on both ends.
choiceNotes: Only VLAN 10 frames would pass, so devices in VLAN 20 could not communicate across the switches.
Communication would work, but the purpose of separating the VLANs (splitting broadcast domains and isolating traffic for security) would be lost.
Correct. With tags, a trunk port carries several VLANs over one link.

network-advanced-006.question: In a network where switches are connected with redundant paths, what role does the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) play?
choices: It logically disables some ports so that the paths form a loop-free tree, preventing broadcast frames from circulating endlessly
It spreads frames evenly over several links between switches to increase bandwidth
It relays frames between different VLANs so that the VLANs can communicate with each other
network-advanced-006.explanation: If switches are connected in a loop, broadcasts and frames to unknown destinations keep circulating and multiplying around the loop (a broadcast storm), and the network stops working. This happens because Ethernet frames have no mechanism like the IP TTL that counts hops and discards the frame. STP has the switches exchange messages called BPDUs and blocks some ports so that the active paths form a tree rooted at the root bridge. If a link in use fails, it moves a blocked port to the forwarding state to switch to another path.
choiceNotes: Correct. It keeps the redundant paths but logically breaks the loop.
That is the role of link aggregation. STP prevents loops by leaving some redundant links unused.
Traffic between VLANs needs routing by a router or L3 switch.

network-advanced-007.question: In STP, the bridge IDs of three switches are known: SW1 has priority 32768 and MAC address 00-00-5E-00-53-01, SW2 has priority 61440 and MAC address 00-00-5E-00-53-05, and SW3 has priority 4096 and MAC address 00-00-5E-00-53-0A. Which switch is elected as the root bridge?
network-advanced-007.explanation: In STP, the switch with the lowest bridge ID becomes the root bridge. The bridge ID puts the priority in the upper part and the MAC address in the lower part, so priorities are compared first and MAC addresses only when the priorities are equal. Here SW3, with the lowest priority of 4096, becomes the root bridge regardless of its MAC address. The default priority is 32768, and if nothing is configured the switch with the lowest MAC address is chosen, so it is common practice to give the switch at the center of the network a lower priority.
choiceNotes: Its MAC address is the lowest, but its priority is higher than SW3's, so it is not chosen.
This switch has the highest priority value. Lower values take precedence.
Correct. Its priority of 4096 is the lowest, so its bridge ID is also the lowest.

network-advanced-008.question: Three switches, SW1, SW2 and SW3, are connected in a triangle with one link between each pair. The STP root bridge is SW1, and SW2 has a lower bridge ID than SW3. All links have the same path cost. Which port is blocked (does not forward frames)?
choices: The port on SW1 that connects to SW3
The port on SW2 that connects to SW3
The port on SW3 that connects to SW2
network-advanced-008.explanation: All ports on the root bridge are designated ports in the forwarding state. SW2 and SW3 each choose as their root port the port with the lowest cost to the root bridge, which is the port connected directly to SW1. On the remaining SW2–SW3 link, both switches have the same cost to the root bridge (one link), so the port on SW2, which has the lower bridge ID, becomes the designated port. The port on SW3 is neither a root port nor a designated port, so it is blocked and the triangular loop is broken.
choiceNotes: Ports on the root bridge are always designated ports and forward frames; they are never blocked.
SW2 has the lower bridge ID, so its port is the designated port on this link and forwards frames.
Correct. It is neither a root port nor a designated port, so it is blocked.

network-advanced-009.question: With default timers, classic STP (IEEE 802.1D) takes about 30 to 50 seconds after a failure before a previously blocked port starts forwarding. Which mechanism lets RSTP switch over faster?
choices: It adds a TTL-like field to frames and discards looping frames after a set number of hops, so ports no longer need to be blocked
Neighboring switches exchange a proposal and an agreement to move ports to forwarding immediately, and alternate ports that can replace the root port are chosen in advance
It uses all links at once to spread frames, so that if any link fails the remaining links keep carrying traffic
network-advanced-009.explanation: Classic STP moves ports to the forwarding state cautiously, waiting on timers so that no loop forms. With the default values, the max age of 20 seconds plus two forward delays of 15 seconds, one each for the listening and learning states, add up to as much as 20 + 15 × 2 = 50 seconds. RSTP has switches connected point-to-point exchange a proposal and an agreement, so a port can start forwarding without waiting for timers. It also chooses in advance an alternate port that takes over when the root port fails, so in many cases the switchover takes a few seconds or less. The basic idea of preventing loops by blocking redundant ports is the same as in classic STP.
choiceNotes: Ethernet frames have no TTL-like field, and RSTP also prevents loops by blocking redundant ports.
Correct. It starts forwarding quickly through exchanges between neighbors, without waiting for timers.
That is closer to the idea of link aggregation. RSTP blocks some of the redundant links.

network-advanced-010.question: Four 1 Gbps links between two switches are bundled into one logical link with link aggregation. Frames are distributed with the common method that chooses the link for each combination of source and destination addresses and port numbers (each flow). Which is closest to the maximum throughput a single TCP connection can achieve?
network-advanced-010.explanation: With link aggregation, frames belonging to the same flow are normally sent over the same single link. Splitting one flow's frames across several links could reorder them and hurt TCP performance. A single TCP connection is therefore limited to one link, 1 Gbps. When there are many flows they are spread over the four links, so up to 4 Gbps can be used in total. If one link fails, traffic continues on the remaining links, and STP sees the bundle as a single link, so none of its member links is blocked.
choiceNotes: Correct. A flow is sent over a single link, so one link's bandwidth is the limit.
A single flow is never split across two links.
This is the total limit when there are many flows. A single connection cannot reach it.

network-advanced-011.question: A router is to be connected with a single link to an L2 switch that has VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24), so that the two VLANs can communicate with each other. Which configuration is appropriate for this setup?
choices: Make the switch port an access port in VLAN 10 and give the router interface a single IP address, 192.168.10.1
Give the hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 addresses from the same subnet so that they can communicate without going through the router

Make the switch port a trunk port, create a subinterface for each VLAN on the router, and configure each with its VLAN ID and the IP address that serves as that VLAN's default gateway (such as 192.168.10.1 and 192.168.20.1)
network-advanced-011.explanation: Traffic between VLANs is relayed at the network layer by a router or L3 switch. To carry several VLANs over one link, the switch side is made a trunk port, and on the router one physical interface is split into a subinterface per VLAN, each configured with an 802.1Q VLAN ID and an IP address. The hosts in each VLAN use the address of their VLAN's subinterface as the default gateway. A packet from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 goes up the link to the router and comes back down the same link with a different tag. This setup is called router on a stick; in networks with many devices, an L3 switch that routes inside the switch is generally used instead.
choiceNotes: Only VLAN 10 frames would reach the router, so hosts in VLAN 20 could not use it.
Different VLANs are separate broadcast domains, so even with the same subnet, ARP would not reach across and the hosts could not communicate.
Correct. With a trunk and subinterfaces, one link routes both VLANs.

network-advanced-012.question: Two routers, R1 (192.168.1.2) and R2 (192.168.1.3), are configured with VRRP using the virtual IP address 192.168.1.254. Normally R1 forwards traffic as the master. Which address should be set as the default gateway on the LAN hosts?
network-advanced-012.explanation: VRRP lets several routers form one virtual router that shares a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC address. Normally the master router forwards packets sent to the virtual address, and if the master fails, a backup router becomes the master and takes over forwarding. If hosts use the virtual IP address as their default gateway, they need no change whichever router is running. Mechanisms like this that make the default gateway redundant are collectively called FHRPs, and besides VRRP they include HSRP and others.
choiceNotes: If R1 fails, hosts configured with this address can no longer communicate outside the LAN.
If R2 fails, hosts lose connectivity, so there is no benefit from redundancy.
Correct. The virtual IP address works whichever router is forwarding.

network-advanced-013.question: 192.168.10.0/24 is to be split into subnets for site A (100 hosts), site B (50 hosts) and site C (25 hosts). Starting with the site that needs the most hosts, each site is given the smallest subnet that holds its hosts, packed in from the lowest addresses. Which subnet is assigned to site C?
network-advanced-013.explanation: A subnet with h host bits holds 2^h − 2 hosts. Site A needs /25 because 2^7 − 2 = 126 ≥ 100, so it gets 192.168.10.0/25 (.0 to .127), and site B needs /26 because 2^6 − 2 = 62 ≥ 50, so it gets 192.168.10.128/26 (.128 to .191). Site C needs /27 because 2^5 − 2 = 30 ≥ 25, so it gets the next block, 192.168.10.192/27 (.192 to .223). Assigning subnets with different prefix lengths like this is called VLSM (variable-length subnet masking). The remaining 192.168.10.224/27 can be split further, for example into /30 subnets for links between routers.
choiceNotes: This is the next block if site B were given a /27. A /27 holds only 30 hosts, so it cannot fit site B's 50.
Correct. After the /25 and /26, a /27 is assigned starting at 192.168.10.192.
A /28 holds only 2^4 − 2 = 14 hosts, so it cannot fit site C's 25.

network-advanced-014.question: Each of the following three sets consists of four consecutive /24 networks. For which set can the four routes be summarized into exactly one /22 route without including any addresses outside the set?
network-advanced-014.explanation: In a /22, the lowest two bits of the third octet fall in the host part, so one /22 consists of four consecutive /24s whose third octet starts at a multiple of 4. For 10.0.4.0/24 to 10.0.7.0/24, the third octet runs from 4 to 7 (00000100 to 00000111 in binary) and the upper 22 bits are common, so they summarize to 10.0.4.0/22. 10.0.2.0/24 to 10.0.5.0/24 straddles 10.0.0.0/22 and 10.0.4.0/22, and 10.0.6.0/24 to 10.0.9.0/24 straddles 10.0.4.0/22 and 10.0.8.0/22, so neither forms a single /22. Summarizing routes (route summarization) keeps routing tables small, but including networks that do not exist pulls in packets that have nowhere to go.
choiceNotes: The smallest route that covers all four is 10.0.0.0/21, not a /22, because 2 is not a multiple of 4.
Correct. They summarize exactly to 10.0.4.0/22.
The smallest route that covers all four is 10.0.0.0/20, not a /22, because 6 is not a multiple of 4.

network-advanced-015.question: A router's routing table has four routes: 172.16.0.0/12 (next hop router B), 172.16.32.0/19 (router A), 172.16.48.0/20 (router C) and 0.0.0.0/0 (router D). To which router is a packet for 172.16.45.10 sent?
network-advanced-015.explanation: A router chooses, among the routes that match the destination, the one with the longest prefix (longest prefix match). The third octet, 45, is 00101101 in binary. A /19 compares the upper 3 bits of the third octet, and 45 AND 224 = 32, so the address matches 172.16.32.0/19 (172.16.32.0 to 172.16.63.255). A /20 compares the upper 4 bits, and 45 AND 240 = 32, which differs from 48, so it does not match 172.16.48.0/20 (172.16.48.0 to 172.16.63.255). The address also matches 172.16.0.0/12 and the default route, but the longest match, the /19, is chosen and the packet goes to router A.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the longest of the matching routes, the /19.
The /12 also matches, but the longer /19 matches too, so it is not chosen.

network-advanced-016.question: Branch router R2 is connected to head-office router R1 over a 10.255.0.0/30 link, with R1's end at 10.255.0.1 and R2's at 10.255.0.2. When a static route to the head-office network 192.168.1.0/24 is configured on R2, which address is appropriate as the next hop?
network-advanced-016.explanation: A static route specifies the destination network and the address of the next router to hand packets to (the next hop). As a rule, the next hop is the address of a neighboring router on a network to which the router is directly connected. Here it is R1's address on the other end of the link, 10.255.0.1, and R2 uses ARP to find the MAC address for it before sending frames. When a branch has only one way out, a common alternative to writing a route for each destination is to configure just one default route, 0.0.0.0/0.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is the address of R1, the directly connected neighbor router.
This is R2's own address, so it cannot be the next router to hand packets to.
This address is not on a network directly connected to R2, and R2 has no route to it, so it cannot be used as the next hop.

network-advanced-017.question: A router has learned routes to the same destination, 192.168.50.0/24, from both OSPF and RIP. On this router, the administrative distance, which expresses the preference for each route source (lower is preferred), is 110 for OSPF and 120 for RIP. Which route goes into the routing table?
choices: Both routes are installed and used alternately for each packet
Only the RIP route is installed
Only the OSPF route is installed
network-advanced-017.explanation: Routing protocols express route quality (the metric) in different ways, such as OSPF cost and RIP hop count, so their metrics cannot be compared directly. When routes to the same destination with the same prefix length are learned from several sources, the router therefore installs the one with the lower administrative distance, a measure of how much each source is trusted. Here OSPF's 110 is lower than RIP's 120, so the OSPF route goes into the routing table. Directly connected networks commonly get 0 and static routes 1, giving lower values to what people configure, but the name and default values differ between equipment vendors.
choiceNotes: Routes from different protocols have metrics with different meanings, so they are not installed side by side and used alternately.
RIP has the higher value and therefore the lower preference, so its route is not installed.
Correct. The OSPF route, with the lower administrative distance, is installed.

network-advanced-018.question: A router's routing table holds three routes: a static route 10.0.0.0/8 (next hop router A, administrative distance 1), 10.1.0.0/16 learned by OSPF (router B, 110) and 10.1.1.0/24 learned by RIP (router C, 120). To which router is a packet for 10.1.1.5 sent?
network-advanced-018.explanation: The three routes have different prefix lengths, so each is installed in the routing table as a separate route. When forwarding a packet, the router chooses the matching route with the longest prefix and does not compare administrative distances. 10.1.1.5 matches all three, but the longest, the /24 RIP route, is chosen and the packet goes to router C. Administrative distance is used only to decide which of several routes to the same destination with the same prefix length goes into the routing table.
choiceNotes: The static route has the highest preference, but the /8 is the shortest match, so it is not chosen.
The /16 also matches, but the longer /24 matches too, so it is not chosen.
Correct. The /24 route, the longest match, is chosen.

network-advanced-019.question: Which statement correctly describes a link-state routing protocol?
choices: Each router builds its routing table only from the destinations and distances (such as hop counts) it receives from neighboring routers
Each router floods the state of its own links so that all routers share the topology of the whole network, and each router computes shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm
An administrator configures routes on each router by hand, and routers exchange no routing information
network-advanced-019.explanation: In a link-state protocol (such as OSPF or IS-IS), each router advertises the state of its links (its neighbors and the costs to them), and all routers in the same area hold the same map. From this map, each router computes a shortest-path tree rooted at itself with Dijkstra's algorithm. A distance-vector protocol (such as RIP) chooses routes by adding its own distance to the "distance to each destination" heard from its neighbors; this is simple, but routers do not know the topology of the whole network and can take time to settle after a failure. Link-state protocols need more computation and memory but react to changes quickly.
choiceNotes: This describes a distance-vector protocol.
Correct. Routers share the whole topology and each computes the shortest paths.
This describes static routing.

network-advanced-020.question: In OSPF, router R1 has three paths to a network beyond R4. Path A uses a 10 Gbps link R1–R5 and a 1 Gbps link R5–R4; path B is a direct 100 Mbps link R1–R4; and path C uses 1 Gbps links R1–R2, R2–R3 and R3–R4. The cost of each link is "reference bandwidth 10 Gbps ÷ link bandwidth", and the cost beyond R4 is the same for all paths. Which path does R1 choose?
network-advanced-020.explanation: The costs are 10 ÷ 10 = 1 for a 10 Gbps link, 10 ÷ 1 = 10 for 1 Gbps and 10 ÷ 0.1 = 100 for 100 Mbps. Path A costs 1 + 10 = 11, path B 100 and path C 10 × 3 = 30, so path A, with the lowest total cost, is chosen. If the reference bandwidth is left at 100 Mbps, long the default on much equipment, every link of 100 Mbps or faster costs 1, giving path A 2, path B 1 and path C 3, and the slowest path, B, is chosen. Networks with fast links therefore set the reference bandwidth to a larger value, the same on every router.
choiceNotes: Correct. Its total cost, 1 + 10 = 11, is the lowest.
It has only one link, but its cost of 100 is the highest. RIP, which chooses by hop count, would choose this path.
Its cost of 10 × 3 = 30 is higher than path A's 11.

network-advanced-021.question: On the internet, which protocol exchanges routing information between the networks run by organizations such as ISPs (ASes, autonomous systems) and chooses routes based on attributes such as the sequence of ASes a route has passed through (AS_PATH) and on each organization's policy?
network-advanced-021.explanation: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol that organizations identified by AS numbers use to exchange routes, and routes on the internet are basically exchanged with BGP. Routes carry attributes such as the sequence of ASes they have passed through (AS_PATH) and the next hop (NEXT_HOP), and a router prevents loops by discarding routes that contain its own AS number. Route selection is not just a matter of the shortest AS_PATH; an organization's policies, such as which neighbor to prefer, can be expressed in attributes and applied. OSPF and RIP are routing protocols used inside a single organization (IGPs).
choiceNotes: OSPF is a protocol that computes shortest paths inside an organization from the state of its links.
Correct. It is the protocol used to exchange routes between ASes.
RIP is a distance-vector protocol that chooses routes by hop count inside an organization.

network-advanced-022.question: Hosts in VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) are to get addresses from a DHCP server, 10.0.0.5, on another network. A DHCP relay agent is therefore configured on the L3 switch interface 192.168.20.1, which is VLAN 20's default gateway. Which statement correctly describes what the relay agent does?
choices: It receives the DHCP messages that hosts broadcast, writes its own VLAN 20 address 192.168.20.1 into them and forwards them by unicast to 10.0.0.5. From this address, the server chooses an address from the range for 192.168.20.0/24
The L3 switch starts forwarding the broadcasts it receives to every network, so the DHCP messages reach the server
The L3 switch chooses addresses and leases them to hosts in place of the DHCP server, only reporting the results to 10.0.0.5
network-advanced-022.explanation: A host that has no address yet broadcasts a Discover to find a DHCP server, but routers and L3 switches do not forward broadcasts to other networks. A DHCP relay agent receives these messages, relays them to the server by unicast, and passes the server's replies back to the host. When relaying, it writes the address of its host-side interface (192.168.20.1 here) into a field of the message (giaddr). From this address, the server learns which subnet the host is on (192.168.20.0/24) and chooses an address from the range for that subnet. This way, a single DHCP server can serve many subnets without a server in every VLAN.
choiceNotes: Correct. It turns the broadcast into unicast and tells the server which subnet the host is on.
A relay agent relays only DHCP messages to a configured server. It does not forward broadcasts in general.
The DHCP server chooses and leases the addresses. The relay agent only relays.

network-advanced-023.question: Which DNS resource record specifies the mail server that receives email addressed to a domain?
network-advanced-023.explanation: An MX record gives the server that mail for a domain is delivered to, as in "mail for example.com is received by mail.example.com." Several servers can be registered with preference values, and delivery is tried starting with the server with the lowest value. A CNAME record defines an alias, used for example to make www.example.com an alias of web.example.net. NS gives the domain's authoritative DNS servers, and A and AAAA give IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, respectively.
choiceNotes: A CNAME record registers one name as an alias of another name.
An NS record gives the authoritative DNS servers that hold the domain's information.
Correct. An MX record gives the server that mail is delivered to.

network-advanced-024.question: Which statement correctly describes how recursive and non-recursive (iterative) queries are used in DNS name resolution?
choices: A host (stub resolver) sends a recursive query to a full-service resolver asking for the final answer, and the full-service resolver sends non-recursive queries to the root servers and authoritative DNS servers, following the referrals to the next server to ask
A host itself repeats non-recursive queries in turn to a root server, a TLD server and the authoritative DNS server to get the answer
Root servers accept recursive queries and, on behalf of the host, query down to the authoritative DNS server and return the final answer
network-advanced-024.explanation: A recursive query is a request to "return the final answer," and a host normally sends this kind of query to a full-service resolver (caching DNS server) run by its ISP or organization. If the answer is not in its cache, the full-service resolver sends non-recursive queries to a root server, a TLD server and the domain's authoritative DNS server. A server that receives such a query returns the answer if it knows it, and otherwise returns a referral (such as NS records) saying "ask this server next." Root and TLD servers do not accept recursive queries, for reasons of load and security.
choiceNotes: Correct. Queries between the host and the resolver are recursive, and those between the resolver and each server are non-recursive.
Walking down the hierarchy is the full-service resolver's job. A host's stub resolver normally sends just one query to the resolver.
Root servers do not accept recursive queries; they only refer the resolver to TLD servers.

network-advanced-025.question: For a web server move, the IP address in the A record for www.example.com will be changed. The record's TTL is currently 86400 seconds, and to keep the time the old address is used after the change to about 5 minutes at most, the TTL will be lowered to 300 seconds beforehand. Resolvers cache records exactly for their TTL. Which is the correct deadline for lowering the TTL?
network-advanced-025.explanation: A resolver that queried just before the TTL was lowered keeps the record cached for the old TTL of 86400 seconds, or 24 hours. Twenty-four hours after the TTL is lowered to 300 seconds, therefore, every resolver's cache holds the new record with the 300-second TTL. If the address is changed after that point, the old address is used for at most about 300 seconds (5 minutes). Once the change is complete and stable, the TTL is raised back to its original value to reduce the number of queries.
choiceNotes: With only 5 minutes, answers cached earlier with the 86400-second TTL can remain for almost 24 hours after the change.
With only 1 hour, answers cached earlier can remain for up to 23 hours after the change.
Correct. Once the old TTL of 86400 seconds (24 hours) has passed, every cache holds the record with the short TTL.

network-advanced-026.question: A router that performs NAPT (outside address 198.51.100.7) is configured with port forwarding, a static setting that translates only the destination: "forward traffic arriving at outside TCP port 8080 to port 80 on the inside web server 192.168.1.20." When host 203.0.113.9 on the internet connects from source port 51000 to port 8080 on 198.51.100.7, which is the destination and source of the packets the web server receives?
network-advanced-026.explanation: With port forwarding, the router rewrites the destination of packets arriving for the outside address and port (198.51.100.7:8080) to the configured inside address and port (192.168.1.20:80). The source is not rewritten, so to the web server the packets appear to come from 203.0.113.9:51000, and its access logs record the client's real address. The server's replies pass through this router, its default gateway, which looks up its translation table and rewrites the source back to 198.51.100.7:8080 before returning them to the client. Connections started from outside have no entry in the translation table under ordinary NAPT and never reach the inside, so this setting is needed to publish a server on the inside.
choiceNotes: This is the destination as sent by the client, before the router rewrites it.
Correct. Only the destination is rewritten to the inside server's address and port.
The setting translates only the destination, so the source is not rewritten.

network-advanced-027.question: An ACL that checks incoming packets from the top is applied to a router interface. Rule 1 is "permit traffic to TCP port 443 on 10.0.0.10," rule 2 is "deny all traffic from source 192.168.1.0/24," and rule 3 is "permit traffic from source 192.168.0.0/16 to TCP port 80"; there are no other rules. Of the four packets (i) "from 192.168.1.5 to TCP port 443 on 10.0.0.10," (ii) "from 192.168.1.5 to TCP port 80 on 10.0.0.20," (iii) "from 192.168.2.5 to TCP port 80 on 10.0.0.20" and (iv) "from 192.168.2.5 to TCP port 22 on 10.0.0.20," which choice lists all the packets that are let through?
network-advanced-027.explanation: An ACL compares a packet with the rules from the top, decides to permit or deny it by the first rule that matches, and does not look at any later rules. A packet that matches no rule is discarded by an invisible "deny all" rule at the end (the implicit deny). Packet (i) matches rule 1 and is permitted. Packet (ii) also fits rule 3, but it matches rule 2 (source 192.168.1.0/24) first and is denied. Packet (iii) matches neither rule 1 nor rule 2 and is permitted by rule 3, and packet (iv) matches no rule and is discarded by the implicit deny.
choiceNotes: Correct. (i) is permitted by rule 1 and (iii) by rule 3; (ii) is dropped by rule 2 and (iv) by the implicit deny.
(ii) matches rule 2 before rule 3, so it is denied. Rules are checked from the top, and the first match decides.
(iv) matches no rule. Packets that match no rule are discarded by the implicit deny.

network-advanced-028.question: In IPv6, which range holds link-local addresses, which are used only within the same link and are always configured automatically on every interface that uses IPv6?
network-advanced-028.explanation: Link-local addresses are in the range fe80::/10; they are not forwarded beyond a router and are used only for communication within the same link. They are used for exchanges such as Neighbor Discovery (NDP) and router advertisements, and a host's default gateway is also normally the router's link-local address. 2001:db8::/32 is a range reserved for examples in explanations and documents (documentation addresses). ff00::/8 holds multicast addresses; IPv6 uses multicast instead of broadcast.
choiceNotes: This is the range of documentation addresses, reserved for use in examples in explanations and documents.
This is the range of multicast addresses.
Correct. fe80::/10 holds link-local addresses.

network-advanced-029.question: In IPv6 SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration), how does a host create a global unicast address?
choices: It queries a DHCPv6 server and leases a 128-bit address managed by the server for a set period

It combines the /64 prefix in the router advertisement (RA) sent by a router with an interface ID (the lower 64 bits) it creates itself, and uses the address after checking that no other device has the same address
It puts its own IPv4 address as it is into the lower 32 bits and fills the upper bits with a value starting with fe80
network-advanced-029.explanation: With SLAAC, a host learns the prefix of its link (normally a /64) from the router advertisements (RAs) that routers send periodically or on request. It combines this with an interface ID, either in the EUI-64 format derived from its MAC address or based on a random value, to form an address. Before using it, the host uses Neighbor Discovery to check that no other device is using the same address (duplicate address detection, DAD). The link-local address of the router that sent the RA becomes the default gateway, and because no server manages the address assignments, it is called "stateless." DNS server addresses are provided by an RA option or by stateless DHCPv6.
choiceNotes: This is address assignment by stateful DHCPv6.
Correct. It combines the RA prefix with an interface ID it creates itself.
No such method exists. Addresses starting with fe80 are link-local addresses, not global unicast addresses.

network-advanced-030.question: An interface with MAC address 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E creates an address with SLAAC from the prefix 2001:db8:1:1::/64 and an interface ID in the EUI-64 format. Which address results?
network-advanced-030.explanation: In the EUI-64 format, the 48-bit MAC address is split into its upper 24 bits and lower 24 bits, and FF-FE is inserted between them to make 64 bits. Inserting it between 00-1A-2B and 3C-4D-5E gives 00-1A-2B-FF-FE-3C-4D-5E. In addition, the second-lowest bit of the first byte (the U/L bit) is inverted, so 00 becomes 02, giving 02-1A-2B-FF-FE-3C-4D-5E. Grouping this into 16-bit pieces and dropping leading zeros in each gives 21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e, and with the prefix the address is 2001:db8:1:1:21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e. Because an address that reveals the MAC address makes the host easier to track, most current operating systems use interface IDs based on random values.
choiceNotes: Correct. FF-FE is inserted and the U/L bit is inverted.
This is the value without inverting the U/L bit. The leading 00 becomes 02.
This inserts FE-FF instead. The bytes inserted are FF-FE, in that order.

network-advanced-031.question: Two sites that run only IPv6 are to be connected through a network that runs only IPv4, and the traffic between the sites should remain IPv6 packets. Which method is appropriate?
choices: Give the hosts at the sites IPv4 addresses as well, making them dual stack, and have them communicate between the sites over IPv4
Increase the MTU on the routers in the IPv4 network so that they forward the IPv6 packets as they are
Build a tunnel in which the routers at each site's exit put IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets for the journey and take them out at the other site
network-advanced-031.explanation: A tunnel carries packets of one protocol inside the data part of packets of another protocol. In an IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel, the routers in the IPv4 network see ordinary IPv4 packets, so the traffic can be carried even though the equipment along the way does not support IPv6. Dual stack runs both IPv4 and IPv6 on one device and is widely used while IPv4 and IPv6 coexist, but in this case the traffic between the sites would be IPv4. A tunnel adds headers, so the packets that can be carried inside it are smaller by that amount.
choiceNotes: The traffic between the sites would be IPv4, which does not meet the requirement that it stay IPv6.
Routers that run only IPv4 cannot interpret and forward IPv6 packets, whatever the MTU.
Correct. IPv6 packets are carried inside IPv4 packets.

network-advanced-032.question: In traceroute, what value is the TTL in the IP header set to in the packet sent to make the fourth router from the source return an ICMP Time Exceeded message?
network-advanced-032.explanation: Each router decreases the TTL by 1 when it forwards a packet, and when the TTL reaches 0 it discards the packet and returns an ICMP Time Exceeded message to the source. A packet sent with a TTL of 4 has 3 left after the first router, 2 after the second and 1 after the third, and reaches 0 at the fourth, so the fourth router returns the message. traceroute sends packets while raising the TTL one step at a time, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and from the source address and timing of the returned messages it shows the routers along the path and their delays in order. When packets reach the destination, it learns that it has finished from the destination's reply (an ICMP echo reply, or a message saying the destination port could not be reached).
choiceNotes: With a TTL of 3, it reaches 0 at the third router, and the third router returns the message.
Correct. The TTL reaches 0 at the fourth router.
With a TTL of 5, 1 is left at the fourth router, which forwards the packet, and the fifth router returns the message.

network-advanced-033.question: Running traceroute from a host to web server 198.51.100.80 showed, on lines 1 to 5, 192.168.1.1, 10.0.0.1, "* * *" (no response), 203.0.113.1 and 198.51.100.80, in that order, and the web server could be used without problems. Which is the most appropriate interpretation of line 3?
choices: The third router forwards packets but is configured not to return ICMP messages when the TTL reaches 0, or limits how many it returns
Packets are discarded at the third router, and in fact none reach the fourth router or beyond
Packets are encrypted only on the section through the third router, so its address cannot be read and * is shown
network-advanced-033.explanation: Responses come back from the routers from the fourth onward and from the destination, so packets are being forwarded past the third router. The third line shows * because that router is configured not to return ICMP Time Exceeded messages, or because it limits how often it sends ICMP to protect its own load. Each line of traceroute shows only the messages returned by the router at that position, so a * along the way does not necessarily mean there is a problem with communication. Conversely, if every line from some point on shows *, packets may be failing to get through around there.
choiceNotes: Correct. The routers beyond it and the destination respond, so the third router is forwarding and simply not returning messages.
The fourth router and the destination respond, so packets do get past the third router.
A * in traceroute means that no response came back within a set time; it has nothing to do with encryption.

network-advanced-034.question: In IPv4, a packet with a total length of 4000 bytes (a 20-byte header and 3980 bytes of data) is split up (fragmented) on a link with an MTU of 1500 bytes. The fragments also have 20-byte headers, and fragmentation is allowed. What is the value of the fragment offset field in the last fragment?
network-advanced-034.explanation: Each fragment can hold MTU − header = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes of data, which is a multiple of 8 and can be used as it is. The 3980 bytes of data are split into three pieces of 1480, 1480 and 1020 bytes. The fragment offset gives the position in the original data in units of 8 bytes, so it is 1480 ÷ 8 = 185 for the second fragment and 2960 ÷ 8 = 370 for the third. The last fragment has a total length of 1040 bytes, and its MF flag is 0 to show that no more fragments follow. The destination puts fragments with the same identification in order of their offsets to reassemble the original packet.
choiceNotes: This is the offset of the second fragment.
Correct. It starts at byte 2960 of the data, so 2960 ÷ 8 = 370.
This is the number of bytes from the start itself. The offset field counts in units of 8 bytes.

network-advanced-035.question: A host communicates with a distant web server through a site-to-site VPN tunnel. TCP connections can be established and small pages load, but large file downloads stall partway. The MTU inside the tunnel is 1400 bytes, and the server sends 1500-byte packets with fragmentation prohibited (the DF bit set to 1). The firewall in front of the server is also set to discard all ICMP. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: The TCP receive window is too small, so not enough data can be sent at once
The ICMP messages saying that fragmentation is needed, sent by the router that discards the oversized packets, do not reach the server, so the server cannot make its packets smaller
network-advanced-035.explanation: In path MTU discovery, the source sends packets with the DF bit set to 1, and a router that discards a packet larger than its MTU reports the size that can pass in an ICMP message (Fragmentation Needed in IPv4, Packet Too Big in IPv6). If the firewall discards these messages, the server keeps sending large packets that are discarded every time, so only large data transfers stall (a path MTU black hole). Connection setup and small responses use packets smaller than 1400 bytes, so they get through without problems. Fixes are to stop discarding these ICMP messages, or to have the router at the tunnel entrance rewrite the TCP MSS to a smaller value. Taking the IPv4 and TCP headers as 20 bytes each, an MTU of 1400 bytes calls for an MSS of 1400 − 20 − 20 = 1360 bytes.
choiceNotes: If name resolution failed, connections could not be established and even small pages would not load.
A small receive window slows transfers but does not make them stall, and it has nothing to do with packet size.
Correct. Without the ICMP messages, path MTU discovery cannot work, and only the large packets keep being discarded.

network-advanced-036.question: Which statement correctly describes DSCP in the IP header, used in QoS control?
choices: It is a 6-bit value indicating how a packet should be treated (its class), and equipment along the path uses it to decide treatment such as putting voice packets in a queue that is sent with priority
It is a value giving the maximum number of routers a packet may pass through, decreased by 1 at each router
It is a value for checking the header for errors, which each router calculates and compares when it receives the packet
network-advanced-036.explanation: DSCP uses the upper 6 bits of the ToS field in the IPv4 header (the Traffic Class field in IPv6) to indicate which class of traffic a packet belongs to. Equipment at the edge of the network sets the value according to the type of traffic (marking), and routers and switches along the path vary their choice of queue and the order in which packets are dropped according to the value. For example, voice, which is sensitive to delay and its variation, is often given EF (value 46), which is forwarded with priority. QoS does not add bandwidth; it decides which traffic to favor, and which to delay or drop, when the network is congested.
choiceNotes: Correct. Equipment along the path decides treatment such as priority from the DSCP value.
This describes the TTL (the hop limit in IPv6).
This describes the IPv4 header checksum.

network-advanced-037.question: On a 70 Mbps outgoing link of a router, three queues are served by weighted round robin with weights 4:2:1. All three queues always have packets waiting, and all packets are the same size. Which is closest to the bandwidth available to the queue with weight 2?
network-advanced-037.explanation: In weighted round robin, each round sends as many packets from each queue as its weight. One round sends 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 packets, two of which come from the weight-2 queue, so its bandwidth is 70 × 2/7 = 20 Mbps. The weight-4 queue gets 40 Mbps and the weight-1 queue 10 Mbps, and when a queue is empty the others can use its share. With strict priority queuing, which always sends from the highest-priority queue first, the other queues cannot send at all when the priority queue is busy. A common combination is therefore to give strict priority only to small amounts of traffic such as voice and to divide the rest by weights.
choiceNotes: This is the bandwidth of the weight-1 queue.
Correct. 70 × 2/7 = 20 Mbps.
This divides the link equally into three (70 ÷ 3), ignoring the weights.

network-advanced-038.question: Using SNMP, a router interface's 64-bit counter of received bytes is read every 5 minutes (300 seconds). The previous reading was 1,200,000,000 and the current one is 4,950,000,000. Which is closest to the average receive rate over these 5 minutes?
network-advanced-038.explanation: The interface received 4,950,000,000 − 1,200,000,000 = 3,750,000,000 bytes in 5 minutes, or 3.75×10⁹ × 8 = 3×10¹⁰ bits. Dividing by 300 seconds gives 1×10⁸ bit/s, or 100 Mbps. In SNMP, the managing side (the manager) queries MIB values from the agent on the device and, as here, works out traffic from differences between counter readings to draw graphs. A 32-bit counter wraps back to 0 after 2^32 ≈ 4.29×10⁹ bytes, which at 100 Mbps takes only about 344 seconds, so 64-bit counters are used for fast interfaces.
choiceNotes: This value does not convert bytes to bits (it is 12.5 MB/s).
This divides the difference by 60 seconds instead of 300.

network-advanced-039.question: For the traffic passing through a router, you want to find out how many bytes are taken up by each combination of source and destination (addresses, port numbers and protocol), aggregated per stream of traffic. Which mechanism is the most appropriate to use?
network-advanced-039.explanation: NetFlow, and IPFIX, the standard based on it, record the packet count, byte count, times and so on for each group of packets with the same source and destination addresses, port numbers and protocol (each flow), and send the records to a collector server. They are used to find which hosts or applications are using bandwidth and to spot unusual traffic. SNMP is a protocol for querying values such as per-interface traffic and CPU usage on equipment and for having equipment report problems (traps); it cannot tell whose traffic it is. syslog sends events such as links going down or logins as text messages to a logging server.
choiceNotes: SNMP shows totals such as the traffic on each interface, not which source and destination the traffic is between.
syslog sends messages about events on the equipment; it does not aggregate traffic per address combination.
Correct. It records and exports packet and byte counts for each flow.

network-advanced-040.question: From a PC, ping with an IP address reaches a server on the internet, but when a domain name is entered in the browser it shows "server not found" and the web page does not open. Which setting is the most appropriate to check first?
choices: The DNS server address configured on the PC
The default gateway address configured on the PC
The LAN cable connection and the link status
network-advanced-040.explanation: When isolating a problem, you check how far things are working, starting from the lower layers. Since ping with an IP address reaches an outside server, everything from the physical layer, such as the cable, up to IP communication through the default gateway (the network layer) is working. Because only access by name fails, a problem with DNS, which translates domain names into IP addresses, is suspected. Check with a command such as nslookup that the DNS server address configured on the PC is correct and that the server responds.
choiceNotes: Correct. IP communication works and only access by name fails, so name resolution is suspected.
If the default gateway were wrong, ping to a server on the internet would not get through either.
If there were a problem with the cable or link, ping would not get through at all.
